name: Acropolis of Athens
label: Acropolis
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Pnyx' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'The Pnyx Monument East Signboard' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/4423249: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Acropolis' (362 m across).
notes: The ancient citadel above the city.

text.description:
The Acropolis is the ancient citadel standing on a flat-topped rock above Athens. It rises about 150 m above sea level and covers roughly 3 hectares. The best-known building is the Parthenon, and the Propylaea, the Erechtheion and the Temple of Athena Nike stand beside it. Most of what you see today was built in the fifth century BC under Pericles, though people lived on the hill thousands of years earlier. The Parthenon was badly damaged in 1687, when a Venetian bombardment set off gunpowder stored inside it. That is why the temple is a ruin today, and the broken columns add to the picture.

It photographs well because the rock stands apart from the city, so the skyline is easy to read from a distance. A good place to shoot from is the Pnyx, a bare rocky hill facing the Acropolis. From there you get a frontal, fairly symmetrical view with pine trees in the foreground. Guides describe it as quieter than the busier hills. Keep the whole rock in the frame, with the Parthenon on top and a little sky above it. Pines on one or both sides make a natural frame. If you want a different angle, Filopappou Hill shows the Parthenon at about eye level across the valley.
text.geographic_location: The Acropolis stands on its rocky hill in the historic centre of Athens, above the old city.
text.directions_text: From central Athens, head to the Pnyx hill, which lies west of the Acropolis. Check access to the Pnyx before you set off. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the whole rock and the pines in one frame. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the Parthenon on top. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of foreground rock and sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (the bare rocky outcrop of the Pnyx hill, facing the Acropolis). A more frontal, symmetrical panoramic view of the Acropolis with pine trees in the foreground. On the bare rocky outcrop facing the Acropolis. The view is frontal and symmetrical, with pine trees in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the Parthenon up with the centre of the frame, so the rock sits level and balanced. Let a pine branch or trunk fill one side as a frame. If you have time, Filopappou Hill is an alternative with the Parthenon at roughly eye level and the city and sea behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the Parthenon to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale stone keeps its detail and the sky does not wash out. A panorama can work for the full hilltop, but hold the phone steady and turn slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, according to one guide.

text.access_note: The Acropolis itself may be a ticketed site with set visiting rules, and access to the Pnyx can change, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The Pnyx lies west of the Acropolis, so the Acropolis is seen towards the east.
In late afternoon the sun is likely to be behind you at the Pnyx and light the face of the Acropolis.
The Parthenon's stone is pale and can lose detail in bright light, so lowering the exposure may help.
The Acropolis site itself may be ticketed with set visiting rules.

name: Parthenon
label: Parthenon
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Pnyx' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'The Pnyx Monument East Signboard' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/910010406: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Parthenon' (92 m across).
notes: The iconic temple of Athena on the Acropolis.

text.description:
The Parthenon is the great temple to Athena on top of the Acropolis, built between 447 and 438 BC, with the sculpted decoration finished by 432 BC. Its life since then has been busy. It became a Christian church in the late 6th century AD and a mosque after the mid-15th century. In 1687 a Venetian bomb hit it while the Ottomans were using it as a munitions dump, and the explosion severely damaged it. Restoration work has been going on since 1975, so you may spot scaffolding or cranes in your shot.

This view is from the Pnyx, on the north-eastern side of the hill. You look due east across open ground and trees, with the Acropolis and the Parthenon on the skyline and Lycabettus Hill rising behind. It is a calmer, free place to stand, and a good spot to sit for a few minutes with the temple in front of you. The trees and rocks make natural foreground for a phone photo, and the distance lets you fit the whole temple on its rock in one frame.

If you want a different angle, the Areopagus gives a closer, slightly higher view, and Filopappou Hill shows the temple side-on across a valley of pines. Areopagus can get very crowded around sunset. Wherever you stand, keep the phone level, because the temple's horizontal lines show any tilt.
text.geographic_location: The Parthenon stands on the Acropolis, in the historic centre of Athens. The Pnyx is on a neighbouring hill to the west, in the group of rocky hills close to the Acropolis.
text.directions_text: No public transport is listed for this spot, so start from the Acropolis area and walk to the Pnyx hill, as the nearby viewpoints are reached on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the telephoto lens (3x to 5x if your phone has it) to bring the temple closer and compress it against Lycabettus Hill. If you only have the default lens (1x), take one shot with the temple small among the trees and another cropped in afterwards. Avoid the ultra-wide (0.5x), which makes the Parthenon tiny.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Pnyx (northeastern side of the hill). The Acropolis and Parthenon seen due east across open ground and trees, with Lycabettus Hill in the background. From here the Acropolis and Parthenon sit due east across open ground and trees, with Lycabettus Hill in the background.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the Parthenon on one of the upper thirds, with the horizon of the rock on a horizontal line. Use trees or the hillside as a frame at the edge of the picture. If you want a closer or side-on view instead, Areopagus and Filopappou Hill are the alternatives.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the temple to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky stays blue and the stone keeps its colour. Take a few shots in a row, as people and branches move through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon is likely to suit this view, as the sun should be behind you and light the front of the temple. Check the official site for the Acropolis hours if you also plan to go up.

text.access_note: The Pnyx is an open hillside and a free place to stand, but the Parthenon itself is within the Acropolis site, so check the official site before you go if you want to visit it.
claims_not_in_sources: From the Pnyx, which lies west of the Acropolis, the late afternoon sun should be behind a photographer looking east and light the western face of the Parthenon.
The Parthenon is within the Acropolis archaeological site, which may be ticketed or have restricted access.
Scaffolding or cranes may be visible on the Parthenon because of ongoing restoration.
A telephoto lens (3x to 5x) will bring the temple much closer than the default lens (1x) at this distance, and the ultra-wide (0.5x) will make it look very small.

name: Plaka
label: Plaka
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/952120095: the OpenStreetMap point 'Plaka'.
notes: Old neighbourhood of lanes under the Acropolis.

text.description: Plaka is the old neighbourhood of Athens, spread across the northern and eastern slopes of the Acropolis. It is a tangle of narrow lanes and neoclassical houses, so it photographs best as a series of small scenes rather than one big view: a doorway with a bright shutter, a stepped lane climbing towards the rock, a café table under a vine. The area has been lived in continuously since the Neolithic period, and the streets of Adrianou and Tripodon follow lines that go back to ancient times. Adrianou Street is the main route through and splits Plaka into upper Ano Plaka, just under the Acropolis, and lower Kato Plaka, towards Syntagma and Monastiraki. Plaka also includes Anafiotika, built during the reign of Otto by settlers from the island of Anafi, with traditional Cycladic architecture that looks quite different from the neoclassical streets around it. Use the phone icon on the map as your starting point, then wander uphill and let the lanes lead you. Keep an eye out for the way the Acropolis appears at the end of a street. Take your time, as people often stop in the middle of the lanes, and step into a doorway or to the side before you lift your phone.
text.geographic_location: Plaka sits on the northeast slope of the Acropolis in central Athens, between Syntagma Square and Monastiraki Square. Adrianou Street runs through its middle.
text.directions_text: Plaka lies between Syntagma and Monastiraki squares, so head for either of those areas first. If you are coming from further away, get to the Syntagma or Monastiraki side first, then continue on foot uphill towards the Acropolis slope. The phone icon on the map is in the heart of Plaka, so once you are among the lanes, follow the map. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the narrow lanes and steps, then switch to the default lens (1x) for doorways and café corners. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for balconies, tiles and details further up a street.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Turn slowly on the spot and look along each lane, then step back into a doorway or to the side of the lane to leave room for passers-by.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line them up with building edges so the walls stay upright. Look for a lane that leads the eye uphill, and include a neoclassical façade, a shutter or a flowerpot in the foreground. If you reach Anafiotika, try a frame with its whitewashed walls and a patch of sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest wall to set focus, then slide the exposure slider down a little so the sunlit stone keeps its detail and the shaded doorways do not wash out. Use portrait mode for a single detail such as a door handle or a cat on a step.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually quieter and gives softer light in the lanes. Late afternoon into evening suits café scenes and warm walls; switch on night mode once the lights come on.

text.access_note: The lanes are part of a lived-in neighbourhood, but museums and archaeological sites nearby may be ticketed or have restrictions, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning is usually quieter in the lanes of Plaka.
Light in the narrow lanes is often strong and contrasty at midday, with deep shade next to bright walls.
The lanes themselves can be walked freely by the public.
The Acropolis can be glimpsed at the end of some streets in Plaka.
Cafés and street lighting appear in the evening.

name: Erechtheion
label: Erechtheion
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Erechtheion' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/910010334: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Erechtheum' (38 m across).
notes: Temple with the Porch of the Caryatids.

text.description:
The Erechtheion is an ancient Greek temple of the Ionic order on the north side of the Acropolis, mainly dedicated to the goddess Athena. It is best known for the Porch of the Caryatids. The building is also unusual because its layout is lopsided, which sets it apart from other Greek temples. This may be down to the uneven ground or to the several cults it housed. Nobody is sure exactly when it was built. It was traditionally dated to about 421-406 BCE, though more recent work favours the 430s. The surviving building accounts from 409-404 BC allow an unusually secure dating of construction.

It photographs well because the porch gives you a strong foreground subject, and the Parthenon rises directly behind it. Guides single out this angle as the best one for the Caryatids. The recommended approach is to stand on the south side of the porch and shoot north, so the figures sit in front and the Parthenon fills the background. Keep the frame fairly tight on the porch, then take a second, wider shot to show the setting. The figures you see on the temple are replicas, and the originals are in the Acropolis Museum, which is worth knowing if you want to see them close up.
text.geographic_location: The Erechtheion stands on the north side of the Acropolis, in the historic centre of Athens. It and the Parthenon are both on the Acropolis.
text.directions_text: No nearby station or tram stop is listed for this spot. The Erechtheion is inside the Acropolis site in central Athens, on the north side of the hilltop. The phone icon on the map is at the Erechtheion itself. The south side of the Porch of the Caryatids is the viewpoint the guides recommend, and the phone icon on the map does not mark that exact spot. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the Caryatid porch and the Parthenon both fit in one frame. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a closer shot of the figures. Keep the ultra-wide (0.5x) for a different view that takes in more of the surroundings.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For the angle the guides recommend, move to the south side of the Porch of the Caryatids and face north. From there the Caryatid porch is in front of you, with the Parthenon appearing behind it in the same frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the porch on one of the lower thirds, leaving the Parthenon visible above and behind it. Keep the phone level so the columns and roofline stay straight. For a different view, the Propylaea gives a wider shot of the Erechtheion among the other Acropolis monuments. Filopappou Hill shows the whole Acropolis from outside, where the temple is small in frame and a telephoto helps.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework of the porch to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out. Take a few shots, since other visitors often walk through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon, when the sunlight falls from the side and shows the shape of the figures, according to one guide.

text.access_note: The viewpoints are inside the Acropolis archaeological site, which needs a ticket, so check the official site before you go for current access rules and opening times.

name: Temple of Olympian Zeus
label: Temple of Olympian Zeu
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Temple of Olympian Zeus' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/63765671: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Temple of Olympian Zeus' (119 m across).
notes: Giant Corinthian columns near Hadrian's Arch.

text.description: The Temple of Olympian Zeus, also called the Olympieion, is a huge ruined temple in the middle of Athens. Work began in the 6th century BC and dragged on for centuries. It was finally finished under the Roman emperor Hadrian in the 2nd century AD. It once had 104 columns, each about 17 metres tall. Today 16 of the giant columns still stand, which is why the place photographs so well: a row of tall marble Corinthian columns with the Acropolis sitting in the distance behind them. The phone icon on the map is at the middle of the temple site, inside the enclosure. For the classic view of the standing columns with the Acropolis behind, the southeast corner inside the enclosure is a recommended angle. The columns are so tall that you will want to step back and tilt the phone up, or switch to the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) to keep their full height in the frame. If you would rather not go in, you can photograph the columns with the Acropolis behind them from Leoforos Amalias, on the street outside the fence. After dark, Vasilissis Olgas gives a view of the floodlit columns with Hadrian's Arch in the foreground. Entry to the site is ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Athens, about 500 m south-east of the Acropolis, on the line between the Acropolis and Ardittos hill. It lies roughly 700 m south of Syntagma Square.
text.directions_text: Head for the Temple of Olympian Zeus from Syntagma Square, which lies to the north. It is about 11 minutes on foot. From the Acropolis, the temple is to the south-east, about 8 minutes on foot. Enter through the ticketed entrance and walk to the phone icon on the map in the middle of the site, with the southeast corner as the suggested angle for the classic view. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the columns with the Acropolis behind. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you want the full height of the columns, and to the telephoto (2x to 5x, depending on your phone) to bring the Acropolis closer behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For the classic view with the Acropolis behind the columns, guides recommend the southeast corner inside the enclosure. If you stay outside the fence, Leoforos Amalias gives a similar view of the columns with the Acropolis rising behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the Acropolis up between or just above the columns. Put a column or two in the foreground so the scale is clear. At night, try the floodlit columns from Vasilissis Olgas, with Hadrian's Arch in the foreground and the lit Acropolis above and behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the columns to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky stays blue and the marble keeps its detail. At night, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body or a solid railing to keep the phone still.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, for soft golden light on the columns. After dark, the floodlit view from the street works well.

text.access_note: The site is ticketed and closes at night, so check the official site before you go for current entry details, and note that tripods are officially restricted. Hadrian's Arch can be seen from the pavement.

name: Panathenaic Stadium
label: Panathenaic Stadium
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Vasileos Konstantinou Avenue (Βασιλέως Κωνσταντίνου)' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Vasileos Konstantinou Avenue (Βασιλέως Κωνσταντίνου) nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/19023844: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Panathenaic Stadium' (344 m across).

text.description:
The Panathenaic Stadium, also called Kallimarmaro ('beautiful marble'), is a long horseshoe of white marble in the middle of Athens, and it is the only stadium in the world built entirely of marble. A racecourse stood here from the 6th century BC. A stadium followed around 330 BC, and Herodes Atticus rebuilt it in marble by 144 AD with room for about 50,000 spectators. After centuries of neglect it was dug out in the 19th century and hosted the opening and closing ceremonies of the first modern Olympics in 1896. Today it is the finishing point of the Athens Classic Marathon.

For a phone photo, the easiest and most rewarding spot is outside. Go to the small park directly across Vasileos Konstantinou Avenue from the stadium front. From there you can fit the whole pale marble façade into one frame, with the statue of Averoff in the foreground to give it a sense of scale. You don't need to go inside, and the park is free to stand in.

Keep the avenue's traffic to the edges of the picture, or wait for a gap. If you do go inside, the top of the seating gives a wide view down the curve. Another good view is from Ardittos Hill, which looks over the whole stadium with Lycabettus Hill beyond. Check the official site before you go for entry arrangements to the stadium itself.
text.geographic_location: The stadium is in the central Athens district of Pangrati, east of the National Gardens and the Zappeion. It sits in a hollow between the pine-covered hills of Ardittos and Agra.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or bus stops are listed for this spot, so the simplest way is by taxi or hired scooter; ask for the Panathenaic Stadium (Kallimarmaro). If you are in the National Gardens and Zappeion area, the stadium lies to the east, in Pangrati. Aim for Vasileos Konstantinou Avenue and the small park on the opposite side of the avenue from the marble front. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the façade looks natural. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if traffic or railings force you to stand close.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Vasileos Konstantinou Avenue (Βασιλέως Κωνσταντίνου) (small park directly across the avenue from the stadium façade). The full marble façade of the stadium with the Averoff statue in the foreground. From it, walk east to the small park directly across Vasileos Konstantinou Avenue from the stadium front. From that park the whole marble front fits in the frame, with the Averoff statue in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Once you are in the park across the avenue, turn on the gridlines and keep the façade level with the top third line, so the verticals stay straight. Place the Averoff statue low in the frame as a foreground anchor. If you go up Ardittos Hill instead, use the default lens (1x) or a little zoom to show the curve of the horseshoe with Lycabettus Hill behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the white marble to focus, then pull the exposure slider down a little so the stone keeps its detail instead of turning flat white. Take a few shots to catch a gap in the traffic.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or later in the afternoon usually gives softer light on the marble and fewer people in the park.

text.access_note: The park across the avenue is open public space, but entry to the stadium itself may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.

name: Monastiraki
label: Monastiraki Square
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1174589042: large area 'Monastiràki' (888 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Busy square with the Tzistarakis Mosque.

text.description:
Monastiraki is the old flea-market neighbourhood of Athens, and one of the city's main shopping districts. It is a busy tangle of clothing boutiques, souvenir shops and specialist stores, which makes it a good place for lively, colourful street photographs. The area takes its name from Monastiraki Square, and the square takes its name from the Church of the Pantanassa, which stands within it. The name means 'little monastery' in Greek. The main streets are Pandrossou Street and Adrianou Street, and both are worth walking along with your phone ready.

The pictures here come from the details: racks of goods outside shops, signs, awnings and the crowd moving between the stalls. A wider shot of the square gives the sense of place, and the church adds an older note to a modern shopping scene. Take a few steps back from the shopfronts so that people and goods fit together in one frame. Then move in close for a single object, such as a pile of souvenirs or a hand-painted sign. The area is popular with visitors, so expect people in your shots. Use that to your advantage by waiting for a gap, or by letting a passer-by give the picture some scale. Keep your phone in a pocket or a wrist strap while you walk, as busy shopping streets are not the place to be careless with it.
text.geographic_location: Monastiraki is a neighbourhood in the old town of Athens, named after Monastiraki Square. Its main streets are Pandrossou Street and Adrianou Street.
text.directions_text: Take the Athens Metro to Monastiraki Metro Station, which is on Monastiraki Square and is served by Line 1 and Line 3. Follow the shopping streets and you will see the Church of the Pantanassa on the square. The phone icon on the map is about 200 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for street scenes. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the square and the church, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details on market stalls.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 200 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. Take your main shots along the streets as you go.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put a street or a row of shopfronts on one of the lines so the picture has a clear direction. Keep a bright sign or colourful goods in the foreground and let the street fade behind. For a shot of the square, use the ultra-wide with the church in one corner and keep the phone level so the buildings do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of a shop front to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the signs look washed out. In a crowd, a Live Photo helps you choose the best frame afterwards. Portrait mode suits a single object on a stall, such as a lamp or a hat.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day, when the shops are opening, is usually quieter and easier for clear shots. Late afternoon gives softer light along the streets, though it is busier.

text.access_note: The streets and square are open public space, but individual shops and the church may have their own rules, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.
claims_not_in_sources: Early in the day the shopping streets are usually quieter than later on.
Late afternoon light is softer along the streets.
The area is busy with visitors, so people will often appear in photographs.
Going into shops or the church may be subject to their own rules or opening times.

name: Syntagma Square
label: Syntagma Square
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Βουλή των Ελλήνων' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Βουλή των Ελλήνων' (relation/2150086): middle (138 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/16363966: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Syntagma Square' (184 m across).
notes: Central square in front of the Parliament.

text.description:
Syntagma Square is the central square of Athens, and it is a good place to photograph the city's civic life. It takes its name from the Constitution that King Otto had to grant after the uprising of 3 September 1843. The Old Royal Palace, which has housed the Greek Parliament since 1934, faces it across Amalias Avenue. Wide marble steps climb the eastern side of the square. There are shade trees to the north and south and a large mid-19th-century fountain in the middle, so you can build shots with plenty of depth.

The best photograph here is the changing of the guard. It takes place every hour in front of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, between the square and the Parliament. On certain days a larger ceremony with an army band brings most of the 120 Evzones out at 11 am. The ceremony is about movement and detail, so aim for the guards and the building behind them rather than the whole square.

It is an approximate position on the right-hand side of the Parliament steps as you face the building. Arrive a few minutes before the hour so you can get a clear spot, and be patient, because the square can be crowded.
text.geographic_location: In the heart of central Athens, in the Syntagma neighbourhood, directly west of the Parliament and the National Gardens across Amalias Avenue. The square is the meeting point of several busy streets, and Ermou Street, a pedestrian street, leads toward it.
text.directions_text: The Syntagma metro station (lines 2 and 3) lies directly under the square, and the Athens Tram terminal is next to it. If you are coming from elsewhere in the city, a taxi to Syntagma Square is the simplest option. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out individual guards from the crowd. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a wider view of the guards with the Parliament behind them. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are well back and want the whole facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Βουλή των Ελλήνων (the right-hand side of the Parliament steps, as you face the building). The guards walking toward the camera across the steps, with the Parliament behind them, suited to a tighter shot. Look for a spot on the right-hand side of the steps of the Βουλή των Ελλήνων (the Parliament), as you face the building. This is an approximate position, so adjust it to the space available and any local signs. From here the guards should walk towards you with the Parliament behind them. The square itself is behind you, to the west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Go for a tight shot: zoom in on the guards as they approach, with the columns and facade filling the background. Turn on gridlines and keep the guards off-centre so they have space to walk into. For a wider alternative, the square itself (Πλατεία Συντάγματος) shows the Parliament with the Evzones at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, framed by the open space. Ermou Street gives a view down the pedestrian street towards Syntagma.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Switch your flash off, because it is not allowed at the ceremony. Tap the guards to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright facade does not wash out. Try a Live Photo or a short burst to catch the marching step. Keep clear of the guards and do not block their movements.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: On the hour, when the changing of the guard takes place. For the larger ceremony with the army band, aim for 11 am on the days it is held. Ermou Street looks best in low late-afternoon sun.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but the Parliament is not open to the public, and rules near government buildings can apply, so follow any local signs and check the official site before you go for ceremony times.

name: Anafiotika
label: Anafiotika
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Anafiotika' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/3828340298: the OpenStreetMap point 'Anafiotika'.

text.description:
Anafiotika is a tiny neighbourhood of whitewashed, cube-shaped houses tucked under the Acropolis rock, part of the old district of Plaka. It was started in the reign of King Otto by builders from the island of Anafi, who came to Athens to work on the royal palace. Other islanders followed, so the little houses look like a Cycladic village. Only about 45 houses remain, and the lanes up towards the rock are still unnamed. Houses are simply called "Anafiotika 1", "Anafiotika 2" and so on.

It photographs well because so much fits into one frame: blue doors, white walls, steps, potted plants and often bougainvillea, with the Acropolis wall rising straight above the roofs. The lanes are narrow and twisting, so the best pictures are close and tight rather than wide. Look for a door, a textured wall or a flight of steps, and crouch a little so you are shooting upwards at the houses with the rock behind them.

People live here, so be a considerate visitor. Don't sit on steps or walls, don't block the lanes, and don't step into open doorways. Keep your phone away from windows, gates and courtyards, and don't photograph residents. For a wider view with the Parthenon above the rooftops, some guides suggest Stratonos Street (check the exact staircase), and a telephoto shot from Lykavittos is another option.
text.geographic_location: Anafiotika sits in the heart of Athens, within the old neighbourhood of Plaka, on the lower slopes of the Acropolis hill. It lies directly beneath the Acropolis rock.
text.directions_text: Walk in from Plaka, the old neighbourhood Anafiotika belongs to, and check the route on arrival. The phone icon on the map is in Anafiotika itself, so once you are among the whitewashed houses you are there. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for most shots. Try ultra-wide (0.5x) only for steps and lane perspectives where you can't step back. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out doors, plants and textures without pointing the phone at anyone's home.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you can see blue doors, white walls, steps and potted plants, with the Acropolis wall rising directly above the houses.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Get low and angle the phone upwards so the whitewashed houses sit against the Acropolis backdrop. Shoot close and tight on doors, textures and details rather than wide, as wide shots tend to catch other photographers. For a wider view with the Parthenon above the rooftops, some guides suggest Stratonos Street (check the exact staircase), and a telephoto shot from Lykavittos is another option.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Turn on gridlines to keep walls and door frames straight. Tap on a door to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so white walls don't turn grey or blow out against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Before about 9–10am, when the lanes are quiet and the light is soft.

text.access_note: Anafiotika is a residential neighbourhood; please respect residents.

name: Theatre of Dionysus
label: Theatre of Dionysus
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Theatre of Dionysus' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/10973697: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Theatre of Dionysus' (158 m across).
notes: Oldest theatre, on the Acropolis south slope.

text.description: The Theatre of Dionysus is an ancient Greek theatre on the south slope of the Acropolis hill, once part of a sanctuary of Dionysus Eleuthereus. It is a good place for photos because the curved rows of stone seating step down to a flat circular orchestra, and the city spreads out beyond them. Those curves give you strong lines to work with, and a few people on the seats help show the scale. The first orchestra terrace here dates from around the mid- to late-sixth century BC. In the fourth century BC the theatre reached its fullest extent and could hold up to 25,000 people. It then fell into decay and was only identified, excavated and restored in the nineteenth century. The best all-round photo is a wide view from partway up the remaining rows, looking down towards the orchestra with the city behind. Guides suggest early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer on the pale stone and the shadows are gentler. A second option is to shoot from the street called Dionysiou Areopagitou, which gives the seating and stage in the foreground with the Temple of Zeus behind. Filopappou Hill offers a distant, raised view down onto the curved seating.
text.geographic_location: The theatre is on the south slope of the Acropolis hill in central Athens, below the Acropolis. The street Dionysiou Areopagitou runs close by.
text.directions_text: Head for the south side of the Acropolis hill and ask for the Theatre of Dionysus or for Dionysiou Areopagitou. Once you are inside the site, walk up into the seating and stop about halfway up the remaining rows. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole curve of seating and the orchestra into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as individual stone seats or the city beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand in the Theatre of Dionysus itself, halfway up the remaining rows of the seating, facing the orchestra. From here you see a wide view of the curved stone seating and the orchestra, with the city spreading out behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and use them to keep the orchestra near the centre while the curved rows sweep across the frame. Keep your phone level so the seating does not lean. If you want a different view, try the street Dionysiou Areopagitou, which shows the seating and stage with the Temple of Zeus behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sunlit stone to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale marble does not turn white. Try a Live Photo if people are moving across the seats.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and the shadows are fewer. Summer midday sun on the pale stone is harsh.

text.access_note: The theatre is an archaeological site that needs an admission ticket, and some upper paths may be closed at times, so check the official site before you go.

name: National Garden of Athens
label: National Garden
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/11505137: large area 'National Garden' (703 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description: The National Garden is a calm, leafy park of 15.5 hectares in the middle of Athens, tucked behind the Greek Parliament building. Queen Amalia commissioned it in 1838 and it was finished by 1840. It was known as the Royal Garden until 1974. It photographs well because it gives you shade, winding paths and tall trees right next to the busy city. There are also small details to look for: a duck pond, a few busts of notable figures and poets, and scattered ancient remains, mostly Roman, including column drums and a mosaic. Its designer, Friedrich Schmidt, brought in more than 500 plant species, though many struggled in the dry climate. The garden sits between Kolonaki and Pangrati and runs south towards the Zappeion. For a phone, think of it as a place for quiet scenes rather than one big view. Look for a path that curves away from you, light coming through the leaves, or a bench under a tree. Wander in slowly and let the garden show you its corners. The ruins and busts make good close subjects, and the duck pond is an easy place to catch some movement. The garden is open from sunrise to sunset, so plan your visit within daylight.
text.geographic_location: In central Athens, between the districts of Kolonaki and Pangrati, directly behind the Greek Parliament building and stretching south towards the Zappeion.
text.directions_text: Head for the Kolonaki and Pangrati side of the garden. Gates are listed on Leoforos Amalias, Vasilissis Sophias Avenue and Herodou Attikou Street, plus one from the Zappeion side. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for paths, trees and benches, as it looks closest to what you see. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) in more open spots, or to get a tall tree and a path in one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as busts, ruins, ducks or sunlit leaves.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Zappeio Megaron (south end, facing the garden's south entrance). The neoclassical Zappeion hall with its columns and garden greenery in the foreground, with the Acropolis visible in the background. Choose a spot on a path where it bends or opens out, so the path leads the eye into the picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and set a path along one of the lines so it leads into the frame. Put some dark leaves at the edge as a natural frame. Hold the phone low for the ultra-wide to make the trees look taller. For ruins and busts, step in close with 2x or more and keep the background simple.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the leaves to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sunlit patches don't turn white. Try portrait mode for a bust or a flower, and Live Photos for ducks or leaves moving in the breeze.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is lower and softer, but remember the garden is open from sunrise to sunset only.

text.access_note: It is a public park, open from sunrise to sunset; check the official site before you go for any changes.

name: Arch of Hadrian
label: Arch of Hadrian
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hadrian's Arch' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/175107932: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Arch of Hadrian' (17 m across).

text.description:
Hadrian's Arch is a marble gateway that once spanned an ancient road running from the centre of Athens towards the Temple of Olympian Zeus. It is thought to have been put up around 131 or 132 AD, to honour the Roman emperor Hadrian when the nearby temple complex was dedicated. It stands about 18 m high and 13.5 m wide. It is made of Pentelic marble, the same stone family used for the Parthenon, and it was built without mortar, with clamps holding the blocks together. That is a lot of detail for a phone to pick up, and the pale stone catches warm light well.

The arch photographs well because of where it sits. Guides most often recommend its northwest side, looking back towards the Acropolis, where stepping back may show a slice of the rock through the opening. The upper level has columns and three rectangular openings, which give you good lines and layers to frame. Each side carries a carved inscription over the arch. The northwest one, facing the Acropolis, reads "this is Athens, the ancient city of Theseus". The southeast one, facing the Olympieion, reads "this is the city of Hadrian, and not of Theseus".

The arch stands right on the pavement beside a busy avenue with tram tracks, so keep clear of the traffic when you step back for the shot. Take your time and shoot a few versions: one wide, one with the Acropolis through the opening, and one close on the carved stone.
text.geographic_location: In central Athens, beside the Temple of Olympian Zeus, on the busy avenue that runs along the south-eastern side of the Acropolis area. The Acropolis is about 325 metres to the north-west.
text.directions_text: There is no Underground, metro or tram stop right at this spot, so use the Acropolis as your starting point. The arch is about 325 metres to the south-east of it. If you are coming from further away in Athens, go by taxi or hired scooter and ask for the Arch of Hadrian beside the Temple of Olympian Zeus. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from a few steps back, so the whole arch fits with the Acropolis behind. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot step back far enough because of traffic. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the rock of the Acropolis through the opening, or for the carved details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Guides most often recommend the northwest side facing the Acropolis; if the view through the opening is not clear, check the other side along Vasilissis Amalias. Step back a little and, where the view is clear, a slice of the rock appears through the opening. Stay on the pavement and away from the tram tracks and the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on your gridlines and line up the arch's vertical edges with them so it does not lean. Keep the opening in the centre and let the Acropolis rock sit inside it. If you want the arch in the foreground with the Olympieion columns and the Acropolis behind, try the junction at Vasilissis Olgas as a second viewpoint. For a view of the arch's full scale and surroundings, the pedestrian promenade of Dionysiou Areopagitou also works.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the marble to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the pale stone keeps its carved detail and the sky does not turn white. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone against a wall or post to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when warm side-light brings out the carving in the marble. Midday light tends to flatten the stone. The arch is most striking after dark, shot from the pavement.

text.access_note: The arch stands on the public pavement beside a busy avenue, so no ticket is needed to photograph it; the neighbouring temple site is separate, so check the official site before you go if you plan to enter it.

name: Roman Agora
label: Roman Agora
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Αδριανού' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Αδριανού' (way/763490837): point nearest the subject (338 m long).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/11197557: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Roman Agora of Athens' (185 m across).

text.description:
The Roman Agora was a market square built in the Roman period, just north of the Acropolis and east of the older Ancient Agora. It was put up between 27 BC and 17 BC (possibly 10 BC) by Eucles of Marathon, paid for with money from Augustus. Julius Caesar had promised the funds in 51 BC. It has not been fully excavated, but it was an open court ringed by columns, with shops behind a marble colonnade on the west side. The entrance on that side was the Doric Gate of Athena Archegetis, and the Tower of the Winds stands by the eastern gate.

For a phone photo, the best free view is from the street called Αδριανού, on the stretch just before the site entrance. Looking toward the Gate of Athena Archegetis, you get the stone gateway in the foreground with the Acropolis rising behind it. It is a simple, strong picture that says 'Athens' at once. Tour groups gather here, so go early if you want a clear frame. If you also want the octagonal Tower of the Winds, a second viewpoint on Αιόλου shows it from outside the fence with little clutter. Check the details of the site's own entry before you plan to go inside.
text.geographic_location: In central Athens, just north of the Acropolis and east of the Ancient Agora.
text.directions_text: Head for the area just north of the Acropolis, or for the Ancient Agora and walk east, as the Roman Agora lies about 100 metres east of it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the gate with the Acropolis behind it. Try 2x or more if you want the gate tighter, and the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street is busy and you need to fit everything in.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Αδριανού (stretch just before the site entrance, looking toward the Gate of Athena Archegetis). The Gate of Athena Archegetis framed with the Acropolis rising behind it. From here the Roman Agora lies to the south-east, and you are looking toward the Gate of Athena Archegetis with the Acropolis rising behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the gate on one of the vertical lines so the Acropolis sits above it. Hold the phone level so the columns do not lean. For an alternative, the Tower of the Winds can be photographed from Αιόλου, seen over the fence with little clutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the gate to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the sky does not wash out. Take a few shots in a row as people walk through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Before 09:00, when the tour groups have not yet arrived and you get a clearer view of the gate.

text.access_note: The street viewpoints are outside the site and free, but going into the archaeological site needs a ticket, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Using 2x or more makes the Acropolis look larger behind the gate than it does at 1x.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep the sky from washing out in a bright scene.
The ultra-wide lens helps fit the scene into a busy or narrow street.

name: Hellenic Parliament
label: Hellenic Parliament
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q477089: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description: The Hellenic Parliament is the home of Greece's law-making body, and it sits in the Old Royal Palace, looking out over Syntagma Square in central Athens. For a phone photo it works well because the building is a broad, calm, symmetrical block, so it is easy to line up and still reads clearly at a small size on a screen. The open space in front gives you room to step back and fit the whole frontage in. Parliament has met here as the country's supreme democratic institution, and the first national parliament of the independent Greek state was set up in 1843, after the 3 September Revolution forced King Otto to grant a constitution. Today it has seats for up to 300 members of parliament, who are elected for four years. A good set of shots might include one wide view of the whole building, one closer shot of the central entrance and columns, and one with a little of the square around it so people can tell where it is. Keep your phone level and use the gridlines so the building's vertical lines stay straight. Afternoons and evenings are often the nicest time to be here. As this is a working government building, stay on the public side and follow any instructions from staff or guards.
text.geographic_location: The Hellenic Parliament is in central Athens, in the Syntagma area. It occupies the Old Royal Palace, overlooking Syntagma Square.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Syntagma Square in central Athens. Parliament is the large building overlooking the square. The phone icon on the map is about 75 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole frontage. If the building feels too small in the frame, step closer or use 2x. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you move very close, and keep the building centred so its edges do not lean or stretch.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 75 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the building's horizontal base with a gridline and its centre with the middle line. Keep your phone upright so the walls do not lean inwards. Then zoom to 2x-5x, if your phone has it, for a tighter shot of the entrance and columns.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the stonework keeps its detail. Take a few shots in case a passer-by walks into the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon to early evening usually gives the warmest light on the front of the building. After dark, use night mode and hold your phone steady against something solid.

text.access_note: The building is a working seat of government, so check the official site before you go if you want to know about visits or access around it.
other_notes: The stand-here point lies on the Syntagma Square side of the building, so the photo looks at the main frontage.
The front of the building faces roughly west, so afternoon and evening light tends to fall on it.
Parts of the area around the building may be restricted, and guards or staff may give instructions.

name: Tower of the Winds
label: Tower of the Winds
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ρωμαϊκή Αγορά' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Ρωμαϊκή Αγορά Αθηνών' (relation/11197557): middle (185 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/11199493: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Tower of the Winds' (18 m across).
notes: Octagonal ancient clock tower in the Roman Agora.

text.description:
The Tower of the Winds is an eight-sided marble tower standing inside the Roman Agora in Athens. It is named after the eight large carved figures of wind gods around the top of its walls, one for each side. The tower is about 12 metres tall and roughly 8 metres across, built of Pentelic marble and raised on three steps. It was finished by about 50 BC at the latest. It once held a water clock and had sundials on its faces, and it is the only clock tower from classical antiquity that still survives. That mix of clean geometry, weathered carving and a long history makes it an easy subject for a phone.

The shape does most of the work. Because the tower is an octagon, you can see two faces at once from almost any corner, which gives the picture depth. The wind reliefs run in a band near the top, and the lines of the sundials are still visible on the walls below. Guides single out the southeast corner of the site as the best angle. From there the reliefs catch low, warm light, and on clear days the Acropolis sits behind the tower.

The best views are inside the Roman Agora, which is a ticketed site, so check the official site before you go. If you would rather not pay, the pavement along Αιόλου (Aiolou Street) outside the site gives a clean, uncluttered view. It is further from the tower, though, so you will need to zoom in. Late afternoon or early morning light suits the marble best.
text.geographic_location: The tower stands inside the Roman Agora archaeological site in Athens. The site is bordered by Αιόλου (Aiolou Street) on one side.
text.directions_text: Head for the Roman Agora in Athens. Once inside the site, the tower is the large octagonal marble building. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from a few steps back so the whole octagon fits. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to the base and want the full height. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the wind reliefs near the top.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (southeast corner of the Roman Agora site). The octagonal tower from the southeast, with the wind reliefs catching low, warm light and the Acropolis behind on clear days. For the angle guides recommend, walk round to the southeast corner of the site, where the reliefs catch the light and the Acropolis can show behind the tower on clear days. Inside the site you can also reach the base and the eastern faces. If you would rather not enter, a free alternative is the pavement on Αιόλου (Aiolou Street), outside the site.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower's vertical edges up with them so the walls do not lean. Choose a corner so that two faces show and the building looks three-dimensional. Leave a little sky above the top, or let the Acropolis sit behind the tower. For a close-up, use the telephoto and frame one or two wind figures together with a sundial line below.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Marble can fool the exposure. Tap the tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the carvings keep their detail. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only when you need it, as it stretches the edges of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the low, warm light shows up the carving. Check the site's opening times first if you are aiming for sunrise or sunset.

text.access_note: The best viewpoint is inside the Roman Agora, a ticketed archaeological site, so check the official site before you go for opening times and entry rules; phone photography needs no permit.
claims_not_in_sources: Αιόλου (Aiolou Street) runs alongside the Roman Agora site; the exact side of the street for the free view is approximate.
Bright marble in strong light can mislead a phone's automatic exposure, so lowering the exposure slider helps.
From a corner of an octagonal building, two faces are usually visible at once.

name: Zappeion
label: Zappeion
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Zappeion' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/9919585: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Zappeion' (164 m across).
notes: Neoclassical hall in the National Garden.

text.description: The Zappeion is a large neoclassical hall on the edge of the National Gardens, and its long colonnaded front is what you come to photograph. The pale stone columns, the symmetry and the open garden in front of it make a calm, balanced picture, and the building is big enough to look impressive even on a small screen. It was designed by the Danish architect Theophil Hansen and opened on 20 October 1888. It was the first building put up specifically for the revival of the Olympic Games, and it served as the fencing hall at the 1896 Games. Today it is used for conferences, exhibitions and ceremonies. Stand on the garden side, in front of the main façade, and shoot straight on. Start low and tilt the phone slightly upwards so the columns rise above the top of the frame. Switch to the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) to fit the whole colonnade and the garden approach. Keep the gridlines on so the columns stay upright and the building looks level. For a second picture, walk into Zappeion Garden and frame the hall behind the fountain, with the water in the foreground leading the eye to the building. This only works when the fountain is running. Another option is the avenue of palms leading in from the Zappeion side of the National Garden, where the light is soft under the trees.
text.geographic_location: The Zappeion is in the centre of Athens, next to the National Gardens and not far from the Temple of Olympian Zeus.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the National Gardens in central Athens and look for the large colonnaded hall on the garden side. By taxi or hired scooter, ask for the Zappeion. The phone icon on the map is at the building itself, so once you reach the garden in front of the main façade you are in the right place. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole colonnade, then the default lens (1x) for a tighter, more natural view. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it for details such as the column tops.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the building is right in front of you. Face it head-on so the full row of columns fills the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone fairly low and tilt it slightly upwards so the columns rise above the top of the frame. Turn on the gridlines and line up the columns with the vertical lines. For a different view, try Zappeion Garden, with the hall framed behind the fountain and the water in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pale stone to set focus and exposure, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the columns keep their detail. Do not zoom in digitally past the telephoto lens, as the picture gets soft.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when warm light falls on the pale stone columns.

text.access_note: The exterior and gardens are open-air, but the interior is used for events and may be closed, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The garden-side view of the main façade works best shot head-on with a wide lens.
Late afternoon gives warm light on the pale stone columns.
The fountain view depends on the water being switched on.
The interior is open mainly on weekdays and may be unavailable because of events.
The National Garden has an avenue of palms leading in from the Zappeion side, with soft filtered light under the trees.

name: Church of Panagia Kapnikarea
label: Kapnikarea
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ermou' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Ermou' (way/86547346): middle (80 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/771404754: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Kapnikarea' (25 m across).
notes: Byzantine church in the middle of Ermou Street.

text.description: Kapnikarea is a small Greek Orthodox church that sits right in the middle of Ermou, one of Athens' busiest pedestrian shopping streets, at the edge of the Plaka district. It is estimated to date from the 11th century, perhaps around 1050, which makes it one of the oldest churches in Athens still in regular use. It photographs well because of the contrast: a stone church with a gabled roof and a dome, framed by modern shop fronts and people walking past. The church was nearly demolished when the new city plan was drawn up in the 19th century, and it was saved after King Ludwig I of Bavaria objected. The building is made up of three parts joined together: the larger south church, a small chapel of St Barbara on the north side, and an entrance porch at the west end. Together they make a layered, slightly uneven outline that suits a wide street view. For the classic shot, walk to Ermou at the west end of the church and look east along the street, so the roof and dome sit between the shop fronts. If you want something tighter, the low wall around the building gives a close view of the roof and dome. Early morning is calmer, and the street gets very busy later in the day. Exterior shots are the simplest choice, because going inside may depend on opening times.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Athens, in the middle of Ermou street, a busy pedestrian shopping street at the edge of the Plaka district.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Plaka district and the shopping street Ermou. The church stands in the middle of Ermou. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the street scene with the church framed by the shops. Switch to 2x or 3x on a telephoto phone for a tighter shot of the roof and dome, or use the ultra-wide (0.5x) from the low wall if you want the whole building in a close space.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Ermou (west end of the church, looking east along the pedestrian street). The church sits in the middle of the pedestrian shopping street, with its gabled roof and dome framed by modern shop fronts. Once there, stand on Ermou at the west end of the church, looking east along the pedestrian street. From here the church sits in the middle of the street, with its gabled roof and dome framed by modern shop fronts. If the street is too busy, try the square called Πλατεία Καπνικαρέας for a street-level scene with the church behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the church centred in the street, so the shop fronts form a corridor on both sides. Hold the phone level to keep the walls upright. For a close alternative, take a shot of the gabled roof and domed centre from the low wall around the building. Wait a moment for a gap in the crowd, or let a few people walk through the frame for scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the church façade to set focus and exposure, then nudge the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright so the stonework keeps its detail. A quick burst or a Live Photo can help you catch a clear moment between passers-by.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when Ermou is quieter. Expect crowds at midday.

text.access_note: The church is an active place of worship, so exterior photos from the street are the simplest option. Opening hours may be limited, so check locally before going inside.

name: Metropolitan Cathedral of Athens
label: Metropolitan Cathedral
camera_source: Commons cluster (15 photos). Moved 20 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 40 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/713354220: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Metropolitan Cathedral of Athens' (60 m across).
notes: Main Greek Orthodox church of the city.

text.description:
The Metropolitan Cathedral, which Athenians simply call the Mitropoli, is the main church of the Archbishopric of Athens and all of Greece. It stands in central Athens, by Mitropoleos Square, and its pale marble walls and domed roof make a calm, solid subject for a phone photo. The cathedral is about 40 m long, 20 m wide and 24 m high. That is big enough to fill the frame from the phone icon on the map, but not so big that you cannot fit the whole building in.

The story behind it adds interest to your pictures. King Otto and Queen Amalia laid the cornerstone on Christmas Day 1842, and the cathedral was dedicated on 21 May 1862. The builders used marble from 72 demolished churches. Next to it, on the south side, stands the little Church of St. Eleftherios, known as the Little Mitropoli. It is worth a second frame, because the small church beside the large one shows the scale well. Mitropoleos Square in front of the cathedral has statues of Constantine XI and Archbishop Damaskinos. A statue in the foreground can give a shot some depth.

This is a working church, so be patient and respectful if a service or ceremony is under way. Keep your phone upright for the full height of the building, then turn it sideways for the wide view. Take a few steps left or right to keep street furniture and passers-by out of the corners.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Athens, beside Mitropoleos Square, with the little Church of St. Eleftherios immediately to the south of the cathedral.
text.directions_text: Make your way to the cathedral in central Athens, near Mitropoleos Square. If you are coming from further away, go by taxi or hired scooter and ask for the Mitropoli. The cathedral lies to the east of it. The phone icon on the map is about 40 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole building in from this close. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look, and to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the dome and the stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 40 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the walls with the vertical lines so the building does not lean. Shoot upright for height and sideways for width. If a statue or the little Church of St. Eleftherios is in reach, include it to add scale and a sense of place.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the marble wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the pale stone does not turn white. If the sky is very bright, tap on the sky and lower the exposure slightly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people in the frame. The light changes through the day, so check how it falls on the walls before you settle on your shot.

text.access_note: The cathedral is a place of worship and a working church, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements and dress expectations.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon light is usually softer, with fewer people around.
As a working church, visitors are usually expected to dress modestly and to be quiet during services.
Some of the statues on Mitropoleos Square may be within reach of the stand-here point to include in the foreground.

name: Choragic Monument of Lysicrates
label: Lysicrates Monument
camera_source: Commons cluster (7 photos), weak. Moved 16 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 20 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Choragic Monument of Lysicrates'.

text.description:
The Monument of Lysicrates is a round monument that stands on a high square base, with slim Corinthian columns around its upper part. A wealthy patron called Lysicrates paid for it to celebrate his chorus winning a music contest at the City Dionysia festival in 335/334 BCE. It is known as the first Greek monument to use the Corinthian order on the outside of a building. Its design was copied so often that you may spot versions of it on towers and memorials around the world.

It photographs well because it is elegant and stands in its own garden on Tripodon Street, so you can frame it cleanly with a calm, simple background. The carved frieze near the top is thought to show the story of Dionysus and the pirates. A second band of carving below it shows prize tripods.

The monument also has an unusual later history. A French Capuchin monastery grew up beside it in the 1600s, and the monks used the monument as a library. In 1818 a friar is said to have planted the first tomatoes in Greece in the monastery garden. The monument was restored in the 1800s.

For your photo, start at the phone icon on the map. Keep the whole monument in view, with its base at the bottom of the frame. Then walk a little closer for detail shots of the columns and the carved band.
text.geographic_location: The monument is in central Athens, near the Acropolis, on Tripodon Street. It stands in a garden of its own beside the street.
text.directions_text: No Metro or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Acropolis area of central Athens and Tripodon Street. Check the official site before you go in case the street or garden has any restrictions. The phone icon on the map is about 20 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the full monument. Switch to the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the carved band and the column tops. The ultra-wide (0.5x) is only useful if you walk right up to it and want to include the whole base and garden.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 20 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. From there the whole round structure, its tall base and the tops of the columns fit comfortably in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the monument on one of the vertical lines, with the base near the bottom third so you don't cut off its feet. Hold the phone level so the columns look straight, not leaning. For a second picture, move closer and use the telephoto to fill the frame with the carved frieze.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the monument to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the monument looks washed out or the sky is bright. If strangers walk into the frame, take a few shots, or use Live Photos and pick the cleanest frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the monument, and quieter streets. At midday the sun can be bright and flat.

text.access_note: The monument is seen from the street, but check the official site before you go for any access rules around the monument and its garden.
